## 1. Interpret the direction and interval

For independent seedlings, the estimated treated-minus-control mean growth
difference is 6.22 mm, with a 95% confidence interval from 2.70 to 9.73 mm.
What quantity is this interval describing? Is it a range for 95% of the plants?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answer

It describes uncertainty in the **population mean difference**, under the
model assumptions and in the stated treated-minus-control direction. It is not
a range containing 95% of individual plants. A 95% confidence procedure covers
the fixed true quantity in about 95% of repeated samples when its assumptions hold.
:::

## 2. What does the p-value condition on?

Does a p-value of 0.0015 mean a 0.15% probability that the null hypothesis is
true, or prove that a 6 mm difference matters biologically?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answer

Neither. It describes the probability, **under the null model and its assumptions**,
of a test statistic at least as extreme as observed. It is not the probability
of the hypothesis. Biological importance needs the effect's size, units,
uncertainty, organism, and purpose. The test cannot repair dependent units.
:::

## 3. Pair by identity

The same ten plants were measured before and after increasing light. Why should
the analysis use within-plant differences? Could independently sorting the two
measurement columns improve their pairing?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answer

The two readings belong to each same plant, so calculate after minus before
within matching IDs. There are ten independent pairs, not twenty independent
plants. Sorting columns independently destroys that identity and does not
improve pairing. The fixed before/after order also leaves a time/order limitation.
:::

## 4. Invert the calibration in the stated direction

The fitted line is approximately
`absorbance = 0.03957 + 0.06489 × concentration_mg_l`.
For an in-range absorbance of 0.310, what formula estimates concentration?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Worked answer

Rearrange to `concentration = (0.310 - 0.03957) / 0.06489`, giving about
**4.17 mg/L**. Use full fitted coefficients in code. We fitted absorbance as
the measured response to known concentration; reversing the regression is a
different fit. The inverse calculation is a point estimate, not full calibration
uncertainty.
:::

## 5. A diluted reading is new evidence

An unknown's original reading is above the measured standards. Can you simply
report the line's extrapolated concentration? If a new in-range reading gives
7.40 mg/L after 1.00 mL was diluted to 10.00 mL total, what is the original estimate?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answer and check

Flag the original as outside range rather than treat extrapolation as a supported
result. A **new** in-range diluted measurement permits a stated correction:
`7.40 × (10.00 / 1.00) ≈ 74.0 mg/L`, using rounded numbers. The dilution assumes
no measured material was lost or reacted. It does not validate another old
out-of-range reading without its own new measurement.
:::

## 6. Slope units and causal limits

A fitted dry-mass-versus-leaf-area slope is about 4.11. Dry mass is in mg and
area in cm². What are the slope's units, and what claim is not established by
this observational fit?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answer

The units are **mg per cm²**: fitted change in dry mass for a one-cm² increase
in area. The sample association does not establish that experimentally changing
area would cause this mass change. Inspect residuals and the measured range,
and avoid extrapolating far beyond observed leaf areas.
:::

## 7. Reversing the contrast

A treated-minus-control95% interval is2.70 to9.73 mm. What is the control-minus-treated interval? What happens to the two-sided p-value?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answer and reasoning

The reversed interval is−9.73 to−2.70 mm. Reverse the endpoint order as well as their signs. The two-sided p-value is unchanged because the equal-means question and observations are the same. Clearly label the reported direction.
:::

## 8. Different confidence levels, same observations

With identical data and model, would a99% interval normally be narrower or wider than a90% interval? Does changing the interval level alter the observed means?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answer and reasoning

The99% procedure gives the wider interval to target greater long-run coverage. The sample means do not change. Retain the confidence level chosen for the main analysis.
:::

## 9. What if the smaller study has a narrower interval?

The transfer study has 9 plants per group instead of 12, yet its interval is narrower. Must R have failed?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answer and reasoning

No. Interval width also depends on observed variability and model assumptions. The transfer study has lower observed group spread. When several features differ, sample size alone does not determine the ordering of interval widths.
:::

## 10. Pairing checked only by means

Independently sorting before and after columns preserves their separate means. Does that validate the paired analysis?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answer and reasoning

No. It destroys subject identity and can alter the spread of within-subject changes while preserving their average. In the actual ten-plant file the correct and artificial pairings have the same mean change but very different SDs and intervals. Sort complete rows together or match by recorded identity.
:::

## 11. A new instrument gives two unknown readings

Transfer standards cover measured signals0.024–0.525. X1 reads0.270 and X2 reads0.700. Which gets an inverse estimate, and what should happen to the other record?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answer and reasoning

X1 is within the measured range and estimates about 2.48 mg/L using the new fitted coefficients. X2 remains in the output with its reading, an out-of-range flag, and no supported concentration estimate. A suitable new measurement is required.
:::

## 12. A unit conversion changes a slope

A mass-on-area slope is4.11 mg/cm². Area is converted to mm² by multiplying by 100. What happens to slope and fitted masses?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answer and reasoning

The slope becomes about 0.0411 mg/mm², a factor of 100 smaller numerically. The intercept and fitted masses remain the same apart from rounding. The biological association did not become weaker merely because the predictor unit changed. A line through formula-calculated values is also not independent empirical evidence.
:::
